an4.30:8.2: This phrase occurs regarding different teachings at [mn117:38.1]() and [sn22.62:13.2](). The commentary says this phrase refers to two individuals named Vassa and Bhañña from a distant land on the Bay of Bengal, Ukkalā (Sanskrit _oḍra_, modern Odisha). But this seems quite unlikely. Ukkalā was distant and largely unknown, mentioned only once elsewhere in the Pali canon ([pli-tv-kd1:4.2.1]()). These teachers with their odd names (“Rain” and “Speak”) appear nowhere else, yet the the phrase _yepi te ahesuṁ_ suggests they were well known; it is elsewhere used only of “those who were” Buddhas of the past. There seems no reason the Buddha should abruptly allude to such obscure figures as if they were an authority. Perhaps read _ukkalā_ from root _kal_ (“to sound”) with prefix _ud_ (“up”), “with raised voice”, cf. Sanskrit _kalabhāṣin_ (“with pleasing voice”). Then _vassa_ from _vṛṣa_ (“bull, chief”), for which compare the expression, _uḷārā āsabhī vācā bhāsitā_, “spoke a lofty bull’s word”, i.e. made a proud and dramatic statement. _Bhañña_ is used elsewhere of speaking “out of faith” (_pasādabhañña_, [pli-tv-bu-vb-pj4:8.11.8]()) or of the intoned recitation used for Buddhist texts (_sarabhañña_, [ud5.6:18.2]() = [pli-tv-kd15:3.2.1](), [pli-tv-kd15:3.2.1](), [pli-tv-kd22:1.10.5]()). Thus the sense would be, “those who loudly and dramatically assert”. | The text does not say that these people were wanderers. _Paribbājakā_ here is a vocative, as in the previous line, and as consistently at this point in this phrase ([mn51:3.2](), [mn117:38.1](), [an4.21:8.4](), etc.).
